title: Mamdani signs bill to ban horse-drawn carriages in New York City
summary:
Animal rights activists back the new law while workers’ unions oppose the ban over concerns about lost livelihoods

Zohran Mamdani, New York City’s mayor, has

blocks.text: Zohran Mamdani, New York City’s mayor, has signed a bill that will bring the city’s horse-drawn carriage industry to an end by 1 June 2028.

Known as Romanch’s Law, the legislation is named after 18-year-old Indian tourist, Romanch Mahajan, who was killed in June after being thrown from a carriage in Central Park when a horse became startled. The law marks the end of an industry that has operated in the city for more than a century.

The legislation has been divisive, with workers’ unions opposing the ban over concerns about lost livelihoods, while animal rights activists have backed the move, citing longstanding concerns over horse welfare, including cases in which horses have died from exhaustion.

During Thursday’s signing, Mamdani said: “For 150 years, horse-drawn carriages have been a fixture of Central Park. Today, we are bringing that chapter to a close. This industry will come to an end, and we have a responsibility to the workers whose livelihoods depend on it. We will work alongside them to ensure they have the financial support and career opportunities they need to build their next chapter.”

Julie Menin, the New York city council’s speaker, also described the legislation as a historic milestone, saying: “This is a truly historic day for New York City, nearly two decades after the council first considered ending the horse-drawn carriage industry.”

“Today, I’m thinking of Romanch Mahajan, who should still be with us and whose tragic, untimely death reminds us why this legislation was so urgently needed. This law will protect the welfare of horses while ensuring that the hard-working New Yorkers who depend on this industry have the support they need to transition to new employment opportunities,” Menin added.

On Tuesday, the Mamdani administration announced a transition plan aimed at supporting about 200 affected workers, including medallion owners, carriage drivers and stable hands. The city, which will release a full transition plan by April 2027, said it plans to facilitate medallion buy-backs, as well as provide stipends and career assistance.
City officials also said they would engage with the Transport Workers Union, which represents carriage industry workers.

Mamdani’s administration said that city officials will establish a Horse Carriage Worker Industry Program offering job training, career counseling, entrepreneurship support, employer connections and tuition assistance.

The city also said it would commission a feasibility study examining electric carriages and electric pedal-assist bicycles as potential alternatives in Central Park, as well as electric carriages along the park’s perimeter.
